title: How social media comments inform the promotion of mask-wearing and other covid-19 prevention strategies
screen_reason: Qualitative content analysis of 615 Facebook comments on three Montana news outlets' daily COVID-19 case reports (19-22 October 2020). Comments were coded against a priori categories and the paper reports the share falling in the confusion/misinformation category (210, 34.1%) and the conspiracy category (118, 19.2%) of the 615 comments - shares of items classified as misinformation, with an explicit denominator, which §1 CONTENT covers (comments are an eligible item type).

estimates.platform: Facebook (comment threads on the public pages of NBC Montana, The Great Falls Tribune and The Billings Gazette)
estimates.measure_type: % of Facebook comments on Montana news outlets' daily COVID-19 reports coded as confusion/misinformation
estimates.denominator: 615 relevant Facebook comments (207 Billings Gazette, 77 Great Falls Tribune, 331 NBC Montana) retained from 1,108 sampled, after excluding 493 as irrelevant; the first 100 'Most Relevant' comments and nested replies were captured per outlet per day for four days
estimates.definition: Comment coded in the confusion/misinformation barrier category, i.e. one that stated incorrect information about COVID-19 as the motivation for its argument (sub-themes: skewed understanding of case rates, belief COVID-19 is low risk relative to other causes of death, belief masks are ineffective, skewed understanding of death rates, belief masks do more harm than good)
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition of misinformation is given; the operational rule is 'Those coded as confusion/misinformation only stated the incorrect information as motivation for their argument.'
estimates.source_quote: Table 1 Totals of Categories. Theme Relevant Comments n % Benefits (Supportive of precautions) 283 46 Personal Experience with COVID 39 6.3 Barriers (total) 388 63 Confusion/Misinformation 210 34.1 Conspiracy 118 19.2 Efficacy 39 6.3 Cost Concerns 21 3.41 Note. n = 615, including the total relevant comments in all three publications.
estimates.page_loc: Results, Table 1 (Totals of Categories); sub-themes in Table 2
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 'The comments were manually coded by two of the authors independently of each other, and inter-coder reliability was checked at the halfway point of analysis' - one senior investigator and one graduate assistant, using a priori Persuasive Health Message categories with emergent categories added; discrepancies resolved by team discussion. NO reliability statistic is reported, and accuracy was judged against the authors' own reading of public-health evidence rather than a named external standard.
estimates.moderator_quote: The researchers sorted the entire population of comments using the Most Relevant feature on Facebook posts, which places the most active comments first, as determined by the number of reactions ... We then used the online software program ExportComments.com to capture and download the first 100 comments, including the nested sub-threads, in response to the daily case-count report for each of the three selected outlets on each of the four days included in the sample.
estimates.notes: CONTENT because the denominator is comments (items), which §1 lists explicitly; this is not the excluded 'belief in false claims' case, which applies to survey respondents' beliefs rather than to items coded for their content. Comments could be coded into more than one theme, so the table's percentages exceed 100% and this row must NOT be added to the conspiracy row. denom_selection=curated: only the first 100 engagement-ranked ('Most Relevant') comments per post per day were captured, which the authors note are the comments 'seen by the most users' - so the corpus is biased toward the most engaging comments, not a random sample of comments. Frame is purposive (three outlets chosen for reach and political slant, four consecutive weekdays during a case surge) and the authors state it is not representative of the population.

estimates.platform: Facebook (comment threads on the public pages of NBC Montana, The Great Falls Tribune and The Billings Gazette)
estimates.measure_type: % of Facebook comments on Montana news outlets' daily COVID-19 reports coded as conspiracy
estimates.value_raw: Conspiracy 118, 19.2% (of n = 615 relevant comments); Table 4's note instead gives 113 as 'the total comments coded as Conspiracy'
estimates.denominator: 615 relevant Facebook comments retained from 1,108 sampled (first 100 'Most Relevant' comments per outlet per day, four days, three Montana news outlets)
estimates.definition: Comment coded as conspiracy, i.e. making a statement questioning the motivations behind the COVID-19 precautions (sub-themes: precautions are fearmongering / being sheep, COVID-19 over-hyped, the media is lying, cases and deaths intentionally falsified, government pushing agendas, government overreach, hospitals and officials lying)
estimates.misinfo_def: 'to distinguish between them, we only coded comments as conspiracy when they made a statement questioning the motivations behind the precautions'
estimates.source_quote: The confusion/misinformation (34.1%) and conspiracy (19.2%) categories represented more than half (53.3%) of the discussion among those identifying barriers. Because conspiracy and confusion/misinformation arguments tend to be closely connected, to distinguish between them, we only coded comments as conspiracy when they made a statement questioning the motivations behind the precautions.
estimates.page_loc: Results, Table 1 and the paragraph following it; sub-themes in Tables 3 and 4
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-coder manual process (senior investigator plus graduate assistant, independent coding, reliability 'checked at the halfway point', no statistic reported, team adjudication of discrepancies).
estimates.moderator_quote: we analyzed the content of 615 comments posted on the Facebook pages of statewide/regional/local news sites in response to daily COVID-19 updates during the fall 2020 surge of the pandemic
estimates.notes: borderline=true: the conspiracy category is defined by QUESTIONING THE MOTIVATIONS behind precautions, so some comments in it (e.g. 'concern about government overreach/control', 'importance of getting on with life') are opinion or distrust rather than false factual claims - a true statement could be coded here. definition_variant=false because this category is DISJOINT from the confusion/misinformation row by construction, not a stricter/broader version of it; the two must not be summed (the paper's own 53.3% combined figure is a cross-category sum and is barred by R8). Internal inconsistency: Table 1 gives 118 conspiracy comments (19.2%) while the note to Table 4 says 113; the Table 1 figure is used because it is the one paired with the reported percentage and 118/615 = 19.2% exactly.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted (not misinformation shares): Benefits/supportive comments 283 (46%), Barriers total 388 (63%), Personal experience 39 (6.3%), Efficacy 39 (6.3%), Cost concerns 21 (3.41%). Not extracted (sub-themes of the two rows above, i.e. finer breakdowns of the same corpus that would multiply near-duplicate rows): Table 2 confusion/misinformation sub-themes - skewed understanding of case rates 71 (11.5%), COVID-19 low risk compared with other causes of death 59 (9.6%), masks ineffective 57 (9.3%), skewed understanding of death rates 17 (2.8%), masks do more harm than good 6 (1.0%); Table 3 conspiracy sub-themes (8.8% down to 0.7%); Table 4 specific claims WITHIN the 113 conspiracy comments (media creating fear 31.9%, politically driven 23.01%, etc.) - these are within-misinformation composition (within_misinfo_content would be true); Table 5 reasons for mask refusal among the n=61 comments mentioning masks. Not extracted (cited from other sources, barred by R8): Cuan-Baltazar et al.'s 1.8% HONcode compliance and >70% low-DISCERN among 110 COVID-19 websites; Pew figures on perceived censorship; the Treasure State poll figures (76% of Republicans not worried, 51% opposing face-covering orders, 95% of Democrats supportive, etc.); and the Center for Health and Safety Culture national survey comparisons (68% very concerned, 55% always wear masks, 38% think COVID is no different from flu, 43% perceiving government overreach). Note also that the discussion re-describes the same figures loosely and inconsistently ('approximately 63% of our comments indicated they thought the risk of COVID-19 had been overblown', '63% of commenters were opposed to wearing masks', '34% of our commenters voiced misinformation for reasons not to wear a mask', 'only 19% of our commenters suggested government overreach'); Table 1's definitions were used instead, since 63% is the barriers total and 19% is the conspiracy total rather than what those sentences claim.

rob.design: Qualitative content analysis of Facebook comments. Frame: three purposively chosen Montana news outlets (NBC Montana, Great Falls Tribune, Billings Gazette - selected for statewide reach, city size and political slant), four consecutive weekdays (19-22 Oct 2020) during a case surge; comments sorted by Facebook's engagement-based 'Most Relevant' order and the first 100 per post per day captured with ExportComments.com, nested replies included. 1,108 comments sampled, 493 excluded as irrelevant, 615 analysed. Unit of analysis is the comment, not the person: commenters may appear repeatedly, no demographics are available, and the authors state the sample over-represents strong opinions and cannot be generalised (bots/trolls could not be excluded). Coding: two authors independently applied a priori PHM categories plus emergent ones, with inter-coder reliability 'checked at the halfway point of analysis' but no kappa or agreement figure given, and multiple codes allowed per comment (percentages exceed 100%). Ethical review waived (public artefacts).
rob.item6_quote: Because conspiracy and confusion/misinformation arguments tend to be closely connected, to distinguish between them, we only coded comments as conspiracy when they made a statement questioning the motivations behind the precautions. Those coded as confusion/misinformation only stated the incorrect information as motivation for their argument.
rob.item10_quote: Confusion/Misinformation 210 34.1 Conspiracy 118 19.2 ... Note. n = 615, including the total relevant comments in all three publications. Totals may exceed 100% as some comments were coded for more than one theme.
